ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Minneapolis, MN
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Minneapolis for refinery piping, vessels, tanks and steel structures, to code. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Minneapolis, Minnesota
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) in Minneapolis: wall-thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks, and shear-wave examination of welds in plate, pipe and structural steel. Technicians travel to your plant, terminal or fabrication shop with the instruments and calibration blocks the scope needs, work to a written procedure, and report readings and indications against the criteria named in your contract. To scope a job, send a Minneapolis UT quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Minneapolis

The Twin Cities sit at the center of a refining and processing corridor in a state with no oil wells of its own. The Pine Bend refinery at Rosemount and Inver Grove Heights and the St. Paul Park refinery both run on crude delivered by pipeline, and a large share of it is heavy Canadian grades. Heavy crude and long-running process units make wall-loss monitoring a routine job: crude and vacuum unit piping, heater and exchanger shells, tank shells and floors, and the product lines that feed the terminals all accumulate thickness readings at condition monitoring locations (CMLs) year after year.

Away from the refineries, the metro area has power plants and natural gas facilities that bring boiler tubing, steam headers and feedwater piping into planned outages. Food processing is the other large industrial sector in the region, and its equipment is unusually demanding to examine: pasteurizers, evaporators, ammonia refrigeration vessels and stainless process piping all need thickness checks and weld examination. Grain and flour milling along the Mississippi leaves steel silos, bins and bucket elevators, while the river itself brings barge terminals, locks and the cranes and structures that serve them. Highway and rail crossings of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers add steel girders and truss members that sit under state DOT inspection programs.

What UT finds and what it misses

An ultrasonic probe sends a short pulse of sound into the metal and listens for what comes back. Sound reflects from the back wall, from the far side of a weld, and from any flaw that interrupts the path, so the instrument shows how thick the wall is and where something is reflecting inside it. That makes UT the method of choice for internal and external corrosion on a pipe wall, for laminations in plate, and for planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks that run through the thickness of a weld, none of which show on the outside.

The limits are specific. UT needs a surface that the probe can couple to, so loose scale, flaking paint and heavy pitting have to be dealt with first. Coarse-grained material, including cast stainless steel and some austenitic welds, scatters sound and can hide flaws. Rounded porosity reflects weakly and is easy to under-call with a shear wave, which is why many codes still pair UT with another method on critical welds. Very thin wall and tight geometry, such as small-bore piping and nozzle corners, need a technique chosen for the geometry rather than a default setup. A competent technician states these limits in the report instead of leaving them for the reader to discover.

Thickness surveys: how a corrosion survey is run

Most thickness work in Minneapolis refineries and plants is contact pulse-echo measurement, written up under ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797) or the owner's own procedure. The technician calibrates the instrument on a step block made of the same material as the component, checks the zero and the velocity, and takes readings on a marked grid or at each CML. On corroded or pitted surfaces a dual-element probe is the right tool, because its angled elements read the nearest reflector rather than the back wall of a clean plate. Reading from the A-scan, not just the digital number, is how a technician avoids double-echo errors on thin or rough wall.

Hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant, and readings taken above the calibration temperature are corrected for the change in sound velocity. Where the owner keeps a CML database, each reading is matched to its location ID so the corrosion rate can be calculated between campaigns; where there is no database, a grid sketch with numbered points stands in. The same measurement style supports tank shell courses, vessel heads and nozzles, and elbows and tees where erosion concentrates. Locations that cannot be measured, because of insulation left in place or an obstruction, are listed as unreadable rather than quietly dropped.

Shear-wave examination of welds

Weld examination uses an angle-beam probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, that sends a shear wave into the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows. The reference level, either a distance-amplitude curve or a code-defined sensitivity setting, is built on a calibration block holding side-drilled holes or notches, and indications are evaluated against that level. The technician scans for lack of fusion at the bevel, incomplete penetration at the root, cracks, and slag lines, and plots every reportable indication by length, depth and position along the weld.

Typical Minneapolis weld scopes include pressure vessel and process piping repairs after an outage, structural groove welds on fabricated steel, tank shell and floor repair welds, and crane runway or support structures. Where a code permits ultrasonic examination as an alternative to radiography, the substitution is agreed in writing with the owner and, for code work, with the authorized inspector before the job starts. UT alone is not a replacement for visual examination of a weld surface, and it does not replace magnetic particle or penetrant testing for surface cracks.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Minneapolis UT work

ASME Section V governs technique: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials, and Article 23 for thickness measurement. Acceptance comes from the code that built or maintains the item. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 sets ultrasonic examination of welds in vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 with Table 341.3.2 covers process piping, and AWS D1.1 Clause 8 (2020 edition) governs groove welds in structural steel. State bridge work is normally written to AWS D1.5, and pipeline girth welds under PHMSA rules follow API 1104. In-service equipment is run to API 510, API 570 or API 653, with the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplying the NDE data: thickness at CMLs, flaw indications, and the technique used to get them.

Minnesota's boiler and pressure vessel requirements, formerly chapter 183 of Minnesota Statutes and now in chapter 326B, are administered by the state's Department of Labor and Industry, and repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Minnesota also runs its own state-plan occupational safety program, which enforces process safety management at covered sites under 29 CFR 1910.119, including mechanical integrity inspection under recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. These rules decide who may sign off a repair and which records the owner has to keep, so they are worth settling with the owner's inspection group before the crew arrives.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Minneapolis, so technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up and calibrates the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the result, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. The Level III oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your own written practice governs the job, the work can be run to it instead, and the Level III review can be arranged through outsourced Level III consulting.

What the UT report contains

Each report identifies the component and its drawing or line number, the procedure and revision used, the instrument, probe and calibration block with calibration checks, the technician and certification level, and the surface condition and temperature at the time of the examination. Thickness reports carry a numbered grid or the CML list with nominal, previous and current readings. Weld reports list each indication with location along the weld, depth, length and amplitude relative to the reference level, with an accept or reject decision against the named criteria and a sketch showing where it lies. Limitations, such as an area that could not be scanned from both sides, are stated plainly.

Planning a UT job in Minneapolis

Minneapolis weather shapes the job. Winter surfaces can sit well below freezing, which stiffens ordinary couplant and slows instrument displays, so cold-rated couplant, warmed batteries and a way to keep the calibration block at working temperature are part of the plan. Frost and ice on outdoor piping and tank shells must be cleared before a reading means anything. Summer heat and humidity bring the opposite problems: sweating cold lines, hot pipe racks and long shifts in confined vessels. Refinery and utility outage windows in the region are busy, so scopes that need a crew mobilized should be raised early with the plant's turnaround team.

Access matters as much as weather. Plants usually require site orientation, badging and permits before a technician starts, and work in tanks and vessels needs confined-space entry procedures. Crews fly into Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport and drive to the site, or travel by road from within the region, so travel and lodging are built into the quotation rather than left to chance. Insulation removal, scaffolding and surface preparation are normally the owner's responsibility, and agreeing who does what before the crew mobilizes avoids standing time.

UT, MT or PT for your Minneapolis job

Choose by the flaw you are worried about. If the question is wall loss or an internal flaw, UT is the method. If the question is a surface crack in carbon or low-alloy steel, magnetic particle inspection in Minneapolis finds it faster and with better sensitivity to tight cracks. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, or the question is a surface-breaking crack on a machined face, liquid penetrant testing in Minneapolis is the right call. Many jobs use two: UT to size and depth a weld, and MT or PT to confirm the surface. The national ultrasonic testing service page describes the method in more detail.

Training your own UT technicians

If you want your own people to do this work, Atlantis trains technicians in ultrasonic testing through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training. Theory is online, practice runs on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator, and the hands-on practical is completed at the employer's own facility under its written practice. Your employer, not a training provider, certifies the technician. See the Minneapolis NDT training page for the full course path, or check the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker before enrolling.

faq.q: Do you provide ultrasonic thickness testing in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to your Minneapolis site with dual-element probes, step blocks and the right couplant for the job, and the readings are taken on a grid or at your corrosion monitoring locations and reported against your minimum thickness.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Only where the governing code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII each treat ultrasonic examination differently, so the substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work begins.

faq.q: What temperature can UT thickness readings be taken at?
faq.a: Standard probes and couplant suit normal ambient surfaces. Hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant, and readings above the calibration temperature are corrected for the change in sound velocity, with the surface temperature recorded in the report.

faq.q: Is UT affected by Minneapolis winter weather?
faq.a: Yes. Cold stiffens ordinary couplant and slows instruments, so cold-rated couplant and protected equipment are used, and frost or ice is removed from the surface first. Heated enclosures can be the owner's responsibility for long outdoor jobs.

faq.q: Who signs off an API 510, 570 or 653 inspection?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection under those codes. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination, records thickness at your monitoring locations and reports flaw indications, and the owner's inspector uses that data in the evaluation.

faq.q: What does a UT weld report show?
faq.a: Each reportable indication is listed with its position along the weld, depth, length and amplitude relative to the reference level, together with the accept or reject decision, the procedure revision, the instrument and calibration record, and any area that could not be scanned.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing not find?
faq.a: UT has trouble with rounded porosity, coarse-grained or cast material, very thin or complex geometry and surfaces that cannot be coupled. It does not replace magnetic particle or penetrant testing for tight surface cracks, and limits are stated in the report.

faq.q: Who qualifies your ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. A client's own written practice can govern the work when it applies.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for UT in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Send the component list, the code or specification, the expected access and the site dates through the quote request link on this page. We reply within one business day to clarify scope and mobilization.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Minneapolis, MN | MPI Testing
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in Minneapolis for welds, rigging, crane parts and steel structures. On-site yoke and wet MT to code. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Minneapolis, Minnesota
mt.html:
If a weld, hook, shaft or steel member in the Twin Cities needs a surface crack check, Atlantis NDT can send a technician to do magnetic particle inspection (MPI) at your site. The work covers carbon and low-alloy steel welds, rigging and lifting hardware, castings, forgings and fabricated structures, using yokes, prods or wet fluorescent particles chosen for the part. Each examination follows a written procedure and ends in a report that states what was found and which acceptance criteria applied. Ask for a scope through this Minneapolis MT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing is used in Minneapolis

Most of the steel in and around Minneapolis works under fatigue, impact or thermal cycling, and those are the conditions that start surface cracks. The two refineries on the south side of the metro, at Pine Bend and St. Paul Park, are the obvious cluster: carbon steel piping and vessel welds, structural supports for pipe racks, lifting lugs, and the attachment welds on exchangers and columns that are checked after repairs and during outages. Tank farms and product terminals add nozzle and repair welds on shells, and the pumps and compressors that serve them add shafts, couplings and baseplates.

Beyond refining, rail is a major user of magnetic particle work in this region. Freight yards and car repair operations deal with couplers, truck frames, axles and bolster components, where a fatigue crack can be small and critical. Grain handling and milling along the Mississippi leaves steel bin structures, elevator legs and conveyor frames; river terminals use steel cranes and mooring hardware. Metro fabrication shops build pressure equipment, structural frames and process skids, and customers often ask for MT on fillet welds, repair excavations and weld attachments before paint or hydrotest. Highway and rail bridges across the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers carry fatigue-sensitive welded details on stiffeners, cover plates and connection plates.

What MT finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection works because a crack in magnetized steel leaks flux into the air above it. Fine iron particles, applied dry or in a liquid carrier, gather at the leak and outline the crack as a visible line, or as a glowing line under ultraviolet light when fluorescent particles are used. It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps and seams, and some discontinuities lying just under the surface, and it is very sensitive to tight fatigue cracks in steel.

The method has hard limits. It works only on ferromagnetic material, which means carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, brass and nickel alloys cannot be magnetized this way. A crack that runs parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no signal, so a part is examined with the field in two directions. Paint, scale and weld spatter weaken indications, and sharp changes in section or the edge of a weld can create non-relevant indications that a trained technician has to separate from real cracks. MT shows where a crack is on the surface but says nothing reliable about its depth, which is a job for UT or controlled grinding.

Technique: yokes, prods, wet particles and fields

For field work the portable AC yoke is the workhorse. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 lb at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke to lift at least 40 lb; the technician checks the lifting power with a standard weight before use and records it. Prods pass current through the part and suit welds and castings where access is limited, but they can leave arc burns if contact is poor, so owners with critical material may restrict them. Coils and central conductors serve shafts and bolts in a shop. Between two shots the yoke is turned roughly ninety degrees, so cracks in any direction are found.

Visible dry particles in contrasting colors are common outdoors; wet fluorescent suspension is chosen when the highest sensitivity is needed and a darkened area and ultraviolet lamp can be set up. Field indicators or a pie gauge confirm that the field is strong enough and in the right direction. After the examination, the part is demagnetized when residual fields would interfere with welding, machining, bearings or later operations, and cleaned of particles. These details are why a written procedure, not a technician's habit, controls the job.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Minneapolis MT work

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the technique for code work, with ASTM E1444 as the practice and ASTM E709 as the guide. Acceptance varies with the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds and AWS D1.5 for bridge welds, each with its own rules for linear and rounded indications. Castings and forgings are judged against their product specification. In-service equipment follows API 510, API 570 and API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplies the examination results.

The state layer matters too. Minnesota's boiler and pressure vessel requirements, formerly chapter 183 and now chapter 326B of Minnesota Statutes, are administered by the state's Department of Labor and Industry, and the National Board Inspection Code applies to repairs and alterations. For refineries and chemical plants, mechanical integrity under 29 CFR 1910.119(j) calls for inspection to recognized good engineering practice, and MT of weld repairs is a common item in those programs. Confirm with your inspection group whether a repair needs an inspector's sign-off before it is closed.

Who does the work

Technicians are mobilized from outside the city, because Atlantis has no office in Minneapolis. They are qualified under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which Level II technicians set up the equipment, perform the examination and interpret indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the results. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. The Level III review comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Where a plant already has its own written practice and procedures, the crew can follow them; if you need procedures written, written practice development covers that.

What the MT report contains

A report names the component or weld ID, the procedure and revision, the technique (yoke, prods or wet), the particles and carrier, the lifting power or current used, the lighting or ultraviolet intensity checks, and the surface condition. It records the technician and level. Every relevant indication is listed with location and size, together with an accept or reject decision against the named criteria; indications judged non-relevant are noted with the reason. Sketches or photographs show positions on the part, and any area that could not be examined, such as a weld under a bracket, is listed as a limitation.

Planning an MT job in Minneapolis

Temperature drives planning. Minneapolis winters put outdoor steel far below the range that ordinary procedures assume, and wet particle suspensions thicken or freeze while dry powder behaves differently on cold, damp metal, so a procedure written for the lower range, or enclosures and heating, may be needed. In summer, hot surfaces dry carriers quickly and make contrast and removal harder. Humid river-valley air and condensation on cold equipment also interfere with dry powder.

Access and housekeeping decide the rest. A part must be accessible for both field directions, and surface coatings, scale and spatter are normally removed or dressed by the owner before the crew arrives. Fluorescent work needs a dark area, so tank interiors and enclosed shops suit it better than a bright yard. Expect plant badging, orientation and hot-work or confined-space permits, and schedule around refinery and utility outage windows. Technicians fly into Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport or drive in, and travel is included in the scope you are quoted.

MT, PT or UT for your Minneapolis job

For crack-like surface flaws in carbon or low-alloy steel, MT is the first choice. If the metal is stainless steel or aluminum, dye penetrant inspection in Minneapolis takes over. If you need to know how deep a crack runs or whether a weld has internal flaws, UT inspection in Minneapolis is the companion method. The national MT service page and the MT versus PT comparison give more on how the two surface methods compare.

Training your own MT technicians

For in-house capability, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with theory online and the practical completed at your own facility under your written practice. Employers certify their own technicians under SNT-TC-1A. The Minneapolis NDT training page lays out the path, and the ASME Section V Article 7 explainer is a good primer on the standard your procedure will follow.

faq.q: Do you offer magnetic particle inspection in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your Minneapolis plant, yard or shop and examine welds, rigging, castings and structural steel with yokes, prods or wet particles, following a written procedure and the code named in your contract.

faq.q: What materials can be examined by magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys cannot be magnetized this way, so those parts are examined by liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How cold can MT be done in Minneapolis winters?
faq.a: The limit is set by the procedure and the particle and carrier used, not by the yoke. Below the procedure's range, the work needs a qualified low-temperature procedure, heating or enclosures, and the surface temperature is recorded in the report.

faq.q: Why is the part magnetized in two directions?
faq.a: A crack lying along the field direction gives almost no indication. ASME Section V Article 7 therefore calls for two examinations at roughly right angles, so cracks running in any direction are found.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MT better than visible MT?
faq.a: Fluorescent wet particles are more sensitive and suit the most demanding work, but they need a darkened area and an ultraviolet lamp. Visible particles in a contrasting color work well outdoors and on most weld inspections.

faq.q: Does the part need to be demagnetized afterward?
faq.a: When residual magnetism would affect welding, machining, bearings or later operations, yes. The procedure states when demagnetization is required, and the technician checks the residual field and records the result in the report.

faq.q: Can MT tell me how deep a crack is?
faq.a: No. MT shows where a surface or near-surface crack is and roughly how long it is. Depth is established by ultrasonic testing or controlled grinding, so many repairs pair MT with UT.

faq.q: Who is responsible for an API 510, 570 or 653 inspection?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility under those codes. Atlantis carries out the magnetic particle examination and reports the indications, and the owner's inspector decides how the data feeds into repair and fitness decisions.

faq.q: How do I request MT in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Send the component list, applicable code or specification, access conditions and site dates through the quote link on this page. We reply within one business day to confirm scope, technique and mobilization.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Minneapolis, MN | LPT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Minneapolis for stainless, aluminum and alloy welds, tanks and machined parts. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Minneapolis, Minnesota
pt.html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, is the surface crack check for metals that magnetic particle testing cannot handle. Atlantis NDT sends technicians to Minneapolis plants, fabrication shops and job sites to examine stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloy and carbon steel welds, castings and machined parts for flaws that break the surface. Visible and fluorescent systems are both available, run to a written procedure and reported against the acceptance criteria you name. To scope a job, use this Minneapolis PT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Minneapolis

Food and beverage processing is one of the most important industrial sectors around the Twin Cities, and its equipment is largely stainless steel: tanks, jacketed vessels, heat exchangers, sanitary piping and the welds that join them. Cracks and open porosity in those welds can trap product and harbor contamination, so owners and fabricators call for penetrant examination of weld repairs and new fabrication, and PT is the natural choice because austenitic stainless cannot be magnetized. Dairy, brewing, grain-based products and ingredient plants all use similar equipment.

The process industries add their own stainless and alloy scopes. The refineries at Pine Bend and St. Paul Park have alloy piping, stainless cladding and overlay welds, heat exchanger tube-to-tubesheet welds and instrument connections, where PT checks the surface after welding or grinding. Metro machine shops and fabricators make aluminum frames, housings and equipment components; foundries and forge shops need surface checks on non-ferrous castings; and power and utility plants use PT on valve bodies, small-bore connections and weld repairs on alloy components. For carbon steel items near these, PT is also a second opinion on a surface that has been ground to remove a crack.

What PT finds and what it misses

A penetrant is a very thin liquid with a dye. It is applied to a clean surface, left to soak into any opening by capillary action, wiped or washed off the surface, and then drawn back out by a developer that makes the leftover liquid show as a colored line or a glowing line under ultraviolet light. PT finds cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and porosity, but only those that are open to the surface. A flaw sealed under the surface or filled with dirt, oil, paint or smeared metal will not show.

That makes surface condition the main variable. Machining, grinding, shot blasting and wire brushing can smear metal across the mouth of a crack, so a part may need etching or careful cleaning before it is examined. Rough or porous surfaces hold penetrant and produce background that hides real indications. PT works on non-porous metals of any kind and on many ceramics and plastics, but not on porous materials. It gives location and length on the surface, and it does not tell you how deep a flaw goes, which is again a job for ultrasonic testing or controlled removal.

Technique: systems, dwell and temperature

Penetrant systems are classed by type and removal method. Type I is fluorescent and Type II is visible dye; the method describes how excess penetrant comes off, either with water, with an emulsifier, or with solvent. Solvent-removable visible penetrant with a solvent-suspended developer is the usual choice in the field because it is portable and works away from a washing station. Fluorescent systems give higher sensitivity and are used where a dark area and an ultraviolet lamp can be set up, for example on critical machined components or in a shop.

The steps are fixed and written into the procedure: pre-clean and dry, apply penetrant for the required dwell time, remove the excess without removing penetrant from flaws, apply developer, wait the development time, and then examine under the specified light. ASME Section V Article 6 gives the standard temperature range for the part and materials as 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside that range the procedure has to be qualified for the actual temperature. A comparator block checks that the penetrant materials are working. Post-cleaning removes residues, which matters for stainless and nickel alloys in service where chlorides or sulfur could be a concern.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Minneapolis PT work

For code work, ASME Section V Article 6 governs technique, with ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417 as the governing practices. Acceptance depends on the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and the structural or bridge code for steel structures. AWS D1.1 recognizes penetrant examination where the contract specifies it. In-service equipment is examined under API 510, API 570 or API 653, with the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the inspection and Atlantis providing the examination data.

Minnesota's boiler and pressure vessel law, formerly chapter 183 and now part of chapter 326B of Minnesota Statutes, is administered by the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, and the National Board Inspection Code governs repairs and alterations. Food plants add their own requirements, since fabrication standards for sanitary equipment often specify surface condition and weld quality in the purchase order. Process safety management under 29 CFR 1910.119 covers the refineries and chemical sites, and surface examination of weld repairs is a routine part of mechanical integrity records.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in Minneapolis, so technicians travel to your site and work to the written practice that Atlantis maintains under ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians prepare the surface, apply the materials, interpret indications and report; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and the Level III oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your customer has its own procedure or a specific qualification requirement, the job can be written around it, and Level III consulting can help prepare or review the paperwork.

What the PT report contains

The report names the component and weld IDs, the procedure and revision, the penetrant type and method, the manufacturer and batch of the penetrant, remover and developer, and the surface preparation used. It records the part temperature, dwell and development times, and the lighting conditions, and shows the technician and level. Each indication is listed with its position, length and shape, and a decision against the acceptance criteria, with photographs or sketches. A note states any surface that could not be prepared or examined, and any indication that was re-examined after cleaning to see whether it was real.

Planning a PT job in Minneapolis

Temperature is the biggest planning issue for this method. Winter in Minneapolis puts outdoor steel and aluminum well below the 40 degree floor of the standard range, and penetrant that is too cold becomes sluggish and changes its dwell behavior. The job then needs a qualified low-temperature procedure, heated enclosures or warmed parts. Summer heat has the opposite effect: a hot surface dries penetrant before dwell is complete and makes solvent removal hard to control, so the surface may need to be cooled or the procedure adjusted.

Other items should be settled before the crew mobilizes. Surfaces must be clean, dry and free of paint, grease and spatter, and the owner normally handles insulation, scaffolding and coating removal. Food plants may require washdown schedules, sanitary procedures and controlled chemicals, so product-safe penetrant materials and clean-up should be agreed in advance. Plant orientation and permits apply as they would for any other trade, and crews fly into Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport or drive to the site.

PT, MT or UT for your Minneapolis job

Use PT for non-magnetic metals and for surface cracks on parts where the shape makes magnetizing awkward. On carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Minneapolis is usually faster and finds tight cracks more reliably, because it also shows flaws just below the surface. When the question is internal soundness or wall thickness, ultrasonic testing in Minneapolis is the right method. The national penetrant testing page covers the method further, and the ASME Section V Article 6 explainer walks through the standard.

Training your own PT technicians

Companies that want to examine their own parts can train technicians through PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training. Theory is online, the Practical NDT penetrant simulator lets trainees practice, and the hands-on practical takes place at the employer's facility under its written practice. The employer certifies. See the Minneapolis NDT training page for details.

faq.q: Do you provide liquid penetrant testing in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your Minneapolis site and examine welds, castings, machined parts and fabricated equipment for surface-breaking flaws, using visible or fluorescent penetrant to a written procedure and the code named in your contract.

faq.q: Which materials suit dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, carbon steel, many ceramics and some plastics. It does not work on porous material, and it only shows flaws that are open to the surface.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done in cold Minneapolis weather?
faq.a: Only with a procedure qualified for the actual temperature. The standard ASME Section V Article 6 range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, so winter outdoor work usually needs heating, enclosures or a low-temperature qualification.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Penetrant can enter only a clean opening. Paint, oil, scale or smeared metal from grinding and machining can seal a crack, so the surface is cleaned, and sometimes etched, before examination, and the preparation is recorded in the report.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible penetrant leaves a colored line seen in normal light and is common in field work. Fluorescent penetrant glows under ultraviolet light, offers higher sensitivity, and needs a darkened area for the examination.

faq.q: Can PT find flaws below the surface?
faq.a: No. PT shows only discontinuities that are open to the surface. Subsurface flaws need magnetic particle testing on magnetic material, or ultrasonic testing for internal flaws and thickness.

faq.q: Do food-grade requirements affect PT?
faq.a: They can. Food and beverage plants may require washdown schedules, specific cleaning chemistry and controlled residues, so penetrant materials, post-cleaning and access should be agreed with the plant before the crew arrives.

faq.q: Who is responsible for API 510, 570 and 653 inspections?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports the indications, and the owner's inspector uses those findings in repair and evaluation decisions under the code.

faq.q: How do I request PT in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Send the component list, the code or specification, the materials and the site dates through the quote link on this page. We reply within one business day to confirm scope and mobilization.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing Alternatives in Minneapolis, MN | RT
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Minneapolis, UT, ASNT Level III review of radiographs and RT training are available. Ask for a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Minneapolis, Minnesota: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, and that includes Minneapolis. Industrial radiography here is a licensed activity: sources and X-ray equipment fall under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules (10 CFR Part 34) or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers. If you searched for radiography in the Twin Cities, this page explains what Atlantis can do for the same inspection problem and where to go for the rest.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative

For many weld and wall-loss questions that people first assume need radiography, ultrasonic testing gives an answer that the code accepts. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits UT in place of RT only under specific conditions. Whether UT can stand in for radiography on your job is a decision for the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector, and it is made before the work begins and written into the procedure. Atlantis mobilizes technicians to Minneapolis sites for ultrasonic testing in Minneapolis, covering both weld examination and thickness surveys.

UT also has practical advantages on a busy site. It needs no exclusion zone, so adjacent trades keep working, and it finds planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks that radiography can miss when they lie across the beam. Surface methods complete the picture, and the same crew can add magnetic particle inspection in Minneapolis or liquid penetrant testing in Minneapolis on the surface of the same welds.

ASNT Level III radiography services that need no radiation license

Some of the most useful radiography work does not involve exposing anything. Atlantis reviews radiographs, film or digital images, and the technique sheets behind them, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code that applies. A second independent read on disputed indications, a check on whether image quality and coverage meet the requirements, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice are all work that an ASNT Level III can do without handling a source. The review comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

This kind of review suits owners in the Minneapolis area who receive radiographs from a contractor and want a qualified second opinion before accepting a weld, or who are preparing for an audit and need to confirm that records and procedures are consistent. Arrange it through outsourced Level III consulting, or ask about written practice development if the issue is the contractor's qualification program.

Learning radiography theory

Technicians who want to understand radiographic testing, from film and image quality to interpretation, can study the theory with Atlantis online. See the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Hands-on exposure work is a separate matter and depends on licensing, radiation safety training and your employer, so training here covers the subject matter rather than source handling. The Minneapolis NDT training page shows how the course path fits together, and employers certify their own staff under SNT-TC-1A.

How to scope your Minneapolis job

Send the weld list, the code and the reason radiography was requested, through the Minneapolis inspection quote request. We reply within one business day and will say plainly which parts of the job we can do, which depend on a licensed radiography contractor, and where UT or Level III review can close the gap. Atlantis has no office in Minneapolis, so crews are mobilized to your site for the scope agreed.

faq.q: Does Atlantis perform radiographic testing in Minneapolis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. Industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules (10 CFR Part 34) or Agreement State equivalents, and it is not a service we offer in Minneapolis or elsewhere here.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Minneapolis welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 all provide for ultrasonic examination, but substitution is agreed in advance with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector, and it must be written into the procedure.

faq.q: What radiography-related work can Atlantis do without a license?
faq.a: An ASNT Level III can review radiographs and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed indications, and review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Can Atlantis recommend a radiography contractor?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If your job needs radiography, check the contractor's license with your state radiation control program and ask to see their written practice.

faq.q: Can my technicians learn radiographic testing theory with Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers the theory online. Hands-on exposure depends on licensing and radiation safety training through your employer, and the employer certifies technicians under SNT-TC-1A.
